extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media critics, and readers interested in journalism ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and prescribing standards of conduct for opinion-column writing, especially around plagiarism, attribution, and columnist diligence. Focuses on how established columnists should avoid lazy oversight and handle corrections transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and formal correction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a columnist uses another writer's phrasing or idea, they must give credit and issue a formal correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes: "we’re fixing it on the web, to give josh credit, and will include a note, as well as a formal correction tomorrow." Guidance implies both an immediate online fix and a subsequent formal correction in print/official channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plagiarism / preserve originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers must avoid copying others' words or ideas; being accused of plagiarism is extremely damaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states: "No writer wants to be accused of plagiarism–it’s a death knell." This functions as normative guidance: do not appropriate others' phrasing or ideas without attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full transparency when explaining mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: If accused of plagiarism, provide a detailed, specific explanation rather than a vague excuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article demands more detail about Dowd's "my friend did it" explanation: identify the friend, explain mode of communication (phone/email/IM), and provide any records. Vague or evasive explanations are criticized as 'bullshit-y'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and preserve evidence of sourcing conversations
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep records (notes, emails, instant messages) of discussions that inform a columnist’s writing so sources and attributions can be verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asks: "Was the conversation in question over the phone... or was it via email or instant messenger, where perhaps there's an electronic record of the exchange?" Encourages retaining traceable evidence of where ideas originated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal responsibility despite status or privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Established, eminent columnists must not rely on their reputation; they remain responsible for careful sourcing and attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The column argues Dowd "enjoys the privileges that come with her role... grew comfortable... then forgot to be careful." It urges that status does not excuse lapses and that privilege can breed complacency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid laziness — practice diligence in drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should actively guard against laziness in their process (checking sources, phrasing, and origins of ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author concludes: "I think Dowd’s mistake had to do with laziness... Her mistake should remind us all to review where we get lazy, and what our positions make us take for granted." This is an exhortation to procedural care at drafting/editing stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize the uniqueness of phrasing before deciding attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a passage or idea seems 'not that remarkable' or could be phrased in many ways, authors should still consider whether attribution is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece observes the contested sentence: "it's not something that couldn’t have been expressed in a number of different ways," but still questions why Dowd needed help expressing it — implying that perceived obviousness of an idea is not a reliable defense against plagiarism claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify secondary sourcing (friends, interlocutors) for prior exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: If an idea is claimed to have come from a friend or interlocutor, verify whether that person had prior exposure to the original source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dowd's claim that a friend suggested the phrasing prompts the author to ask: "but, clearly, my friend must have read josh marshall without mentioning that to me." This suggests writers should check secondary sources' exposure to original material before assuming originality.
